results.title: Agent Evaluation (Rollouts) — a quick, pragmatic guide to start the design | by HARSH PATHAK | Medium
results.content: # Agent Evaluation (Rollouts) — a quick, pragmatic guide to start the design. Evaluating the rollout of AI agents is a complex process that goes beyond simple query-response metrics and requires analyzing the agent’s entire action sequence, or “trajectory”. Here are the key aspects of evaluating agent rollouts. **Offline evaluation**: This involves testing the agent against a “golden data set” of benchmark input-output pairs before it is deployed to users. * **Trajectory evaluation**: This method analyzes the steps an agent takes to reach a solution. * **Single-step evaluation**: For more complex agents, you can evaluate individual steps in isolation, such as whether the agent selected the appropriate tool for a specific task. **Online evaluation**: This involves continuously monitoring and analyzing the agent’s performance in a real-world, live environment with actual user interactions. * Learn from various benchmarks on how they decompose various tasks and evaluated the success of the AI Agents, recommended reading.

results.title: How to Successfully Transition SaaS Pilots Into Full Rollouts
results.content: # How to Successfully Transition SaaS Pilots Into Full Rollouts. The pilot might showcase automated claims workflows, but without an expansion plan tied to compliance and scale, the insurer shelves it as a "nice experiment." The same happens in B2B marketplaces where a payment reconciliation tool solves friction for a test cohort yet fails to win budget because impact wasn't modeled for the wider ecosystem. A strong SaaS pilot rollout plan should always be viewed as a springboard for adoption and revenue acceleration, never as an isolated experiment. Build a simple case study model that translates measuring pilot success in SaaS into tangible business wins. These moves make scaling SaaS pilot to rollout smoother and more predictable. Organizations can further enhance their approach by implementing proven email automation best practices throughout their pilot and rollout phases. By aligning metrics, structuring for long-term value, and embedding scalable automation, our team can guide you in building pilots that naturally transition into enterprise-wide rollouts.

results.content: 15 Different Types of Designs • Formative/Developmental • Understanding context, selecting, tailoring, and adapting strategies for later testing • Non-experimental • Observational studies (policy) • Within-site designs: • Generally simpler, typically not randomized (compare to pre or to no implementation) • Between-site designs: • Replication/aggregation, comparison of implementation strategies, randomization can reduce bias, produces generalized knowledge • Within- and between-site designs: • Roll-out designs (e.g., stepped wedge) • Randomize timing (and potentially to implementation strategy) Hwang, Birken, Melvin, Rowheder, & Smith, 2020, J Clin Trans Sci 16 Within-Site Designs • Post Design • Pre-Post Design • Interrupted Time-Series • Rarely randomized • Single site can demonstrate feasibility and initial impact (more sites are needed for full evaluation) • Any hybrid approach can be used • Most commonly see either a Type I or a Type III as these designs lend themselves to a primary focus Hwang, Birken, Melvin, Rowheder, & Smith, 2020, J Clin Trans Sci 17 Between-Site/Within- and Between-Site Designs • Novel implementation strategy vs routine practice ​ • Comparative Implementation ​ • Two novel implementation strategies for the same clinical/preventive intervention (7 Ps)​ • Two/Three-arm cluster randomized trials • Roll-out designs (Stepped-wedge) • Factorial designs/SMART • Non-Randomized or Randomized​ • Any hybrid approach can be used • If unit of randomization is patient > Type I (maybe a Type II) • If unit of randomization is clinician/clinic/CBO > Type II/Type III • Exceptions of course because Hybrid approaches are not dictated by trial/study design • Interesting design examples combining cluster and patient-level randomization (Raising Healthy Children, NU IMPACT) 18 1 8 • Matched-pair randomized roll-out trial using a hybrid Type 2 effectiveness-implementation approach • Comparing Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) for depression and anxiety with services as usual • Implementation Strategies • In-person training • Ongoing booster trainings • EHR modifications (for ease of referral and tracking program status) • Audit and feedback from program status tracker • Financial/billing solutions (Wolk et al., 2021, Medical Care) • Illinois law for CoCM reimbursement • Analysis Plan • Effectiveness: CoCM effects on reducing depression/anxiety symptoms (compared to non-enrolled and pre) • Implementation: Reach and adoption (closely examining health equity in outcomes) and sustainability (compared
